query: We aim to synthesize an equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy via ink-extrusion additive manufacturing using a precursor blend of metallic and hydride powders. The process relies on the sequential thermal decomposition of hydrides (TaH0.5, NbH, HfH2, TiH2, ZrH2) to drive alloying, where decomposition temperatures correlate with hydride formation enthalpies. To prevent the formation of alpha-HCP phases induced by dissolved oxygen (an alpha-stabilizer) which would otherwise degrade mechanical properties, the sintering atmosphere must be strictly controlled using an oxygen getter. The goal is to achieve a nearly fully dense microstructure where slow cooling results in a dual-phase (alpha-BCC + beta-BCC) structure, but a rapid quench from the homogenization temperature traps a metastable single-phase beta-BCC structure. Propose a hypothesis for the specific oxygen getter material and sintering regime that balances dehydrogenation kinetics with oxygen scavenging, predict the resulting phase constitution and grain size after rapid quenching, and design a falsification experiment using in-situ X-ray diffraction to verify the sequence of phase transformations and the absence of alpha-Ti during the critical decomposition window.

generation.hypothesis: Using Ti as an oxygen getter in an argon atmosphere during sequential thermal decomposition of TaH0.5, NbH, HfH2, TiH2, and ZrH2 powders will scavenge oxygen released from hydride decomposition and ambient ingress, preventing alpha-HCP phase formation. A rapid quench from the homogenization temperature (1300°C) will trap a metastable single-phase beta-BCC structure with a grain size of 1-5 μm, whereas slow cooling will yield a dual-phase (alpha-BCC + beta-BCC) microstructure. The decomposition sequence follows the order of hydride formation enthalpies: TaH0.5 (lowest T) → NbH → ZrH2 → HfH2 → TiH2 (highest T), ensuring complete dehydrogenation before alloying.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic blend of TaH0.5, NbH, HfH2, TiH2, and ZrH2 powders with initial oxygen content <0.1 wt%
generation.intervention: Ink-extrusion additive manufacturing with Ti powder (5-10 wt%) as oxygen getter, sintering in argon atmosphere at 1300°C for 30 min, followed by rapid water quenching
generation.conditions: Atmosphere: Argon (99.999%); Getter: Ti powder; Decomposition temperatures: TaH0.5 (~300°C), NbH (~400°C), ZrH2 (~500°C), HfH2 (~600°C), TiH2 (~700°C); Quench rate: >100°C/s
generation.structural_mediator: Ti-O solid solution formation and TiO2 precipitation that sequesters oxygen, preventing Ti dissolution into the matrix and subsequent alpha-BCC nucleation
generation.mechanism: Sequential hydride decomposition releases H2 and metallic elements; Ti getter reacts with O2 (from hydride impurities and atmosphere) to form stable TiO2, maintaining low oxygen activity in the melt. Rapid quenching suppresses diffusion-controlled alpha-BCC nucleation, retaining beta-BCC phase.
generation.predicted_outcome: Single-phase beta-BCC microstructure with grain size 1-5 μm after rapid quench; dual-phase (alpha-BCC + beta-BCC) after slow cooling; density >98%; oxygen content <0.05 wt%
generation.baseline: Without Ti getter, oxygen content >0.8 wt% leads to HfO2 precipitation and alpha-BCC formation, reducing ductility and increasing hardness to >500 HV
generation.boundary: Valid for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; fails if getter amount <5 wt% or quench rate <50°C/s; invalid for non-equimolar compositions
generation.uncertainty: Exact decomposition temperatures may vary with particle size and mixing homogeneity; Ti getter efficiency depends on dispersion and surface area; rapid quenching may induce residual stresses
generation.falsification_experiment: Perform in-situ X-ray diffraction during heating from 25°C to 1300°C at 10°C/min in argon with and without Ti getter. Monitor for alpha-Ti peaks (BCC) between 600-800°C (TiH2 decomposition window). Absence of alpha-Ti peaks in the getter-containing sample confirms successful oxygen scavenging; presence indicates getter failure.

cited_evidence.text: The Ta-Nb-Hf-Zr-Ti alloy in the form of buttons was prepared by vacuum arc melting of the nominal mixtures of the corresponding elements. The degrees of purity of Ta, Nb, Hf, Zr, and Ti were 99.9%, 99.9%, 99.7%, 99% and 99.7%, respectively. Melting was conducted in a high-purity argon atmosphere. High-purity molten titanium was used as a getter for residual oxygen, nitrogen, and hydrogen. In order to achieve homogeneous distribution of the elements in the alloys, the buttons were turned upside down and re-melted four times. The buttons were approximately 13 mm thick and 35 mm in diameter and had a shiny surface. Following this stage, the alloys were cast into bars of 9 mm in diameter and 85 mm in length. One group of specimens was left to solidify inside the mold after casting. Namely, it underwent a process of gravity casting. The other group was cast by applying suction by means of a vacuum pump. The last stage was Hot Isostatic Pressing (HIP), HIP is a common practice, involving high temperatures and isostatic pressure and it is used for closing internal porosity [ [12] ].
